abstract: Background: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a life-limiting inflammatory disease characterised by skin and visceral fibrosis. We previously showed that fibrotic skin from patients with diffuse cutaneous SSc (dcSSc) accumulates a large number of somatic mutations, although the mechanisms that generate them and their disease-related consequences remain poorly understood. We investigated the burden, clonal architecture and biological significance of somatic mutations in dermal sections from patients with dcSSc (<2 years from the first non-Raynauds symptom), dcSSc treated with autologous haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (post-AHSCT) and limited cutaneous SSc (lcSSc, <5 years from the first non-Raynauds symptom), together with dermal fibroblasts (DFs) from each group. Methods: We performed whole exome sequencing of 52 lesional skin biopsies and 33 low-passage (passage 2) DF lines with autologous buccal DNA as the germline reference. Dermal samples comprised 20 dcSSc, 22 lcSSc and 10 post-AHSCT biopsies, and 21 DF from dcSSc patients, and 12 in the post-AHSCT group. Mutational burden, signatures and variant allele fractions were related to clinical phenotype, fibroblast transcriptomes and replication timing, and post-AHSCT samples were used to assess persistence of mutant clones. Results: Mutations were carried by clonally expanded dermal cell populations, and represented a median of 17% of sampled cells, without evidence of positive selection. A large component of all mutations (>25 %) had a sequence linked with oxidative guanine damage (C>A), pointing to ongoing DNA damage and cellular stress. The C>A burden was higher in dcSSc than in lcSSc and correlated with the modified Rodnan skin score - a clinical measurement of skin fibrosis severity. Variant burden increased with patient age but not with disease duration. AHSCT did not change the mutational landscape. Conclusions: Fibrosis skin in SSc is characterized by a widespread somatic mosaicism generated by ongoing mutagenesis attributable to oxidative DNA damage. Persistence of mutant clones after regression of fibrosis argues against their being sufficient drivers of the fibrotic phenotype and identifies the somatic genome as a record of cellular injury.
